exam2-review-01.answer: A system with several masses has several frequencies because it can vibrate in several different ways, called **modes**. In each mode the masses move together or against each other in a different pattern, so each mode stretches the springs by a different amount. When the masses move against each other, the springs between them stretch and compress more, so more stiffness is working and that mode vibrates faster. So each mode has its own frequency, and a system with N masses has **N modes and N frequencies**.
teaching: In a two-mass system, two masses sit between two walls and are joined by three springs. A **mode** is one way of vibrating, and the two masses can move **together** or **against each other**, which gives two different modes.

When the two masses move together, the spring between them moves along with them and never stretches, so only the two outer springs are working. When the masses move against each other, the middle spring stretches and compresses too, so all three springs are working.

**More working springs give more stiffness, and more stiffness gives a higher frequency.** That is why the two modes have different frequencies, even though the masses and springs themselves never change.
exam2-review-01.change: He could ask the same question about a membrane such as the vocal folds. He could also ask why the highest mode is the fastest. The reasoning stays the same, so name the modes and explain how much the springs stretch in each one.

exam2-review-02.answer: A 3-mass system has **three modes**. This is because a system with N masses has N modes of vibration.
teaching: A chain of masses joined by springs can vibrate in as many ways as it has masses, so **N masses give N modes**. One mass has one mode, two masses have two modes and three masses have three modes.
Each new mass adds one more pattern of moving together or against its neighbors, so each new mass adds exactly **one more mode**.
exam2-review-02.change: He could give a different number of masses. Four masses give four modes, and six masses give six modes.

exam2-review-03.answer: **Mode 3 has the highest frequency.** In Mode 3 every mass moves against its neighbor, so every spring stretches and compresses as much as possible. That puts the most stiffness to work, and more stiffness pulls the masses back to the middle faster, so Mode 3 vibrates fastest.
teaching: In a 3-mass system, three masses are joined by four springs. In **Mode 1**, all three masses move **together**, so the middle springs hardly stretch and the frequency is the **lowest**.
In **Mode 2**, the **middle mass stays still** while the two outer masses move against each other. The springs stretch more than in Mode 1, so the frequency is **higher**.
In **Mode 3**, the middle mass moves against both outer masses, so **every mass moves against its neighbor**. This mode has the most stretching and compression, so it has the **highest frequency**.
exam2-review-03.change: He could ask which mode has the lowest frequency, and that is Mode 1 because the masses move together. He could also ask about a 4-mass system. The highest mode is always the one where every mass moves against its neighbors.

exam2-review-04.answer: **Mode 1 and Mode 3 go down, and Mode 2 stays the same.** The middle mass moves in Mode 1 and in Mode 3, so its extra weight slows the system and lowers the frequency of both modes. In Mode 2 the middle mass stays still, so its extra weight has **no effect** on that frequency.
teaching: In a 3-mass system, the middle mass is called **Mass 2**. **A mass only changes the frequency of a mode in which that mass moves**, so extra weight on a mass that stays still changes nothing, however heavy it gets.
The answer depends on what Mass 2 does in each mode. Mass 2 **moves in Mode 1 and Mode 3**, so those frequencies go down. Mass 2 **stays still in Mode 2**, so that frequency does not change.

**Perturbation theory** predicts how a small change in one location affects how something vibrates. The same change at one spot affects each mode differently, because the spot moves in some modes and stays still in others.
exam2-review-04.change: He could ask about stiffening a spring instead of adding mass. A spring only changes the frequency of a mode in which that spring stretches, so stiffening a spring that does not stretch in a mode does nothing to that mode. Stiffening a spring that stretches raises that mode's frequency.

exam2-review-05.answer: An infinite number of masses and springs gives a **string**, such as a guitar or piano string. Every small piece of a string has mass, and every small piece acts as a spring that stretches and compresses. So a string vibrates in modes just like a chain of masses, only with an infinite number of modes.
teaching: A chain of masses and springs turns into a **string** when more and more masses and springs are added, all the way to an **infinite number**.
A surface built the same way, such as a **drum** or the **vocal folds**, is called a **membrane**. A membrane is also an infinite number of masses and springs.
exam2-review-05.change: He could ask what a drum or the vocal folds are in these terms. Both are membranes, which are made of an infinite number of masses and springs.

exam2-review-06.answer: Circle the four points inside the string where it crosses its middle line, along with the two fixed ends. At those points the string does not move, but the pieces on each side move in opposite directions. So the string is stretched and compressed the most there, which means those points have the **most springiness**. The tops of the bumps move the most, so they have the least springiness.
teaching: Along a vibrating string, **the places with the most movement have the least stretching, and the places with the most stretching have the least movement**. So motion and springiness alternate along the string.
The **peaks of the bumps** move up and down the most, so they act as mass. The **still points** between the bumps and at the fixed ends do not move, so they are where the springs work hardest.
**Mode 5** of a string fixed at both ends has five bumps. So it has four still points inside the string, plus the two fixed ends.
exam2-review-06.change: He could show a different mode. Mode N of a string fixed at both ends has N bumps and N minus one still points inside the string. The springiness is always at the still points and at the two ends.

exam2-review-07.answer: **Mode 5 has a frequency of 1000 Hz.** In a string fixed at both ends, each mode is a whole-number multiple of the base frequency. So Mode 5 is five times 200 Hz.
teaching: The **base frequency** is the frequency of Mode 1. In a system **fixed at both ends**, Mode 2 is twice the base frequency, Mode 3 is three times the base frequency, and so on.
The arithmetic stays simple, because the frequency of a mode is just the mode number times the base frequency.
exam2-review-07.change: He could give a different base frequency or a different mode. He could also switch to a system fixed at one end and free at the other. Then only odd multiples occur, so Mode 2 is three times the base frequency and Mode 3 is five times the base frequency.

exam2-review-08.answer: The frequencies are evenly spaced whole-number multiples of the base frequency because each higher mode fits a whole number of copies of the first mode into the same length. The first mode is half a wave that goes from no motion at one end to the most motion in the middle and back to no motion. Both ends must stay still, so every mode has to fit a whole number of these half waves. Mode 2 fits two, so it vibrates **twice as fast**, and Mode 3 fits three, so it vibrates **three times as fast**.
teaching: In a system **fixed at both ends**, the multiples come from **counting how many copies of the first mode fit** into each higher mode.
More pieces in the same length make **shorter waves**, so the vibration is faster. So the frequency grows by one base frequency with each new mode.
These evenly spaced frequencies are called **harmonics**. In speech, the vocal folds are the main system fixed at its edges.
exam2-review-08.change: He could ask the same question about a system fixed at one end and free at the other. That system gives odd multiples instead, because its modes are built from quarter-wave pieces that must end with motion at the free end.

exam2-review-09.answer: Draw a frequency axis along the bottom and an amplitude axis going up. Then draw **six evenly spaced spikes at 200, 400, 600, 800, 1000 and 1200 Hz**, one for each mode. If each mode is equally strong, the spikes can be the same height.
teaching: A **spectrum** shows **which frequencies a vibration has and how much amplitude (strength) each one has**. Frequency runs along one axis, and amplitude runs along the other.
A string fixed at both ends has every whole-number multiple of the base frequency. So its spikes are **evenly spaced**, one base frequency apart.
exam2-review-09.change: He could ask for a system fixed at one end and free at the other. Then the spikes fall only at odd multiples, so with a base of 200 Hz they sit at 200, 600, 1000 and 1400 Hz.

exam2-review-10.answer: Draw spikes at **150, 300, 450, 600 and 750 Hz**, with frequency along the bottom and amplitude going up. The vocal folds are a membrane fixed on its edges, so their harmonics are whole-number multiples of F0. So the spikes are evenly spaced, 150 Hz apart.
teaching: **F0** is the base frequency of the vocal folds, which is the frequency of their lowest mode.

The vocal folds are **fixed on their edges**, so they follow the fixed-fixed rule and give **evenly spaced harmonics**. Measurements of real voices in Praat, a program for analyzing speech, show the second harmonic at about double the first.
**Heavier, looser folds give a lower F0**, so their harmonics are closer together. **Tighter, lighter folds give a higher F0**, so their harmonics are farther apart.
exam2-review-10.change: He could give a different F0, and then each spike is a whole-number multiple of that value. He could also ask what happens to the spacing when the folds get tighter or heavier. Tighter folds spread the harmonics apart, and heavier folds pack them closer together.

exam2-review-11.answer: Circle the fixed bottom and the three points where the building crosses its resting position. Those points do not move, but the parts above and below them move in opposite directions. So the structure stretches and compresses the most there, which means those points have the **most springiness**. The free top moves the most and has the least springiness, so it is not circled.
teaching: A building is **fixed at the ground and free at the top**, so it is a **fixed-free system**.
In every mode of a fixed-free system, the **fixed end always has springiness**, and the **free end always has the most motion**.

**Mode 4** holds **seven quarter-wave pieces**. Each piece goes from no motion to the most motion, so between the fixed bottom and the free top there are three more still points where the springiness is greatest.
exam2-review-11.change: He could show Mode 2 or Mode 3 instead. Mode 2 has one still point above the base, and Mode 3 has two still points above the base. In every mode the base is springy and the top is moving.

exam2-review-12.answer: The building is analogous to **the air in the vocal tract**. The air in the vocal tract is fixed at one end and free at the other, just as the building is.
teaching: The air in the vocal tract is **fixed at the vocal folds**, because the closed folds keep the air there from moving. It is **free at the lips**, because the air there moves in and out easily.
The frequencies of vibration of this air are the **formants**, and the formants make the vowels and consonants of speech.
exam2-review-12.change: He could ask the reverse, which is what in the physical world behaves like the air in the vocal tract. The answer is a building, or a string fixed at one end and free at the other.

exam2-review-13.answer: The analogy holds because **both are fixed at one end and free at the other**. A building is fixed to the ground and free to sway at the top. The air in the vocal tract is fixed at the closed vocal folds and free to move at the open lips. Because the ends are held the same way, both have the same kind of modes, with springiness at the fixed end, the most motion at the free end and frequencies at odd multiples of the first.
teaching: Two systems behave alike when they are made of **masses and springs held the same way at their ends**. The materials do not matter, only how each end is held.
**Mode 1** of the air in the vocal tract matches Mode 1 of a swaying building, because both have **no motion at the fixed end and the most motion at the free end**.
exam2-review-13.change: He could ask how the building and the air differ. Engineers design buildings to sway only in Mode 1, but the air in the vocal tract vibrates in all of its modes at once.

exam2-review-14.answer: **Mode 3 goes up and Mode 4 goes down.** In Mode 3 the boxed spot does not move but is stretched the most, so the added mass does nothing and the added stiffness raises the frequency. In Mode 4 the boxed spot moves the most and is not stretched, so the added mass lowers the frequency and the added stiffness does nothing.
teaching: In a system with many masses, raising the mass and the stiffness together does **not** cancel out. This is because **where** the change happens decides which effect counts in each mode.
At a **still point**, only the stiffness matters, so **the frequency goes up**. At a **moving point**, only the mass matters, so **the frequency goes down**.
Each mode has to be checked separately, because the same spot can be still in one mode and moving in another.
exam2-review-14.change: He could move the box or ask about different modes. For each mode, check whether the box sits on a still point or on a peak, and then apply the rule. A still point means the frequency goes up, and a peak means it goes down.

exam2-review-15.answer: **The frequency of Mode 4 goes down.** The top of the building is the free end, so it has the most motion and no springiness. The added mass counts because the top is moving a lot, so it lowers the frequency. The added stiffness does nothing because nothing is stretching there.
teaching: The free end of a fixed-free system **moves the most in every mode**, so a change there acts only through **mass**.
The same thing happens in the vowel /u/. Rounding the lips adds mass at the free end of the vocal tract, where the air moves the most, so the formants go down.
exam2-review-15.change: He could ask about adding mass and stiffness at the very bottom instead. The base never moves but is always springy, so the added stiffness counts and the frequency goes up.

exam2-review-16.answer: The formants are odd multiples because a fixed-free system can only hold an **odd number of quarter-wave pieces**. The basic piece runs from no motion at the fixed end to the most motion at the free end, which is a quarter of a wave. Every mode must start still at the fixed end and end with the most motion at the free end. Adding one more piece would leave a still point at the free end, which is not allowed, so pieces are added two at a time. That gives one, three, five and seven pieces, so the formants are 1, 3, 5 and 7 times the base frequency.
teaching: In a system **fixed at both ends**, the basic piece goes from still to moving and back to still. Both ends are the same, so every whole number of pieces fits.
In a **fixed-free system**, the two ends are different, so **only odd numbers of quarter-wave pieces fit**. So the frequencies jump from one to three to five times the base frequency.
exam2-review-16.change: He could give a base frequency, such as 500 Hz, and ask for the next two formants. They are 1500 Hz and 2500 Hz, not 1000 Hz and 1500 Hz.

exam2-review-17.answer: The **formants** of the air in the vocal tract have these properties. The air is fixed at the vocal folds and free at the lips, so its frequencies of vibration are odd multiples of the first formant.
teaching: **Formants are the frequencies of vibration of a system fixed on one side and completely free on the other.** In speech, that system is the **air in the vocal tract**.

In **schwa**, the vocal tract has no constriction (narrowing), so the formants sit at evenly spaced odd multiples. Every other vowel shifts the formants by making a constriction somewhere in the tract.
exam2-review-17.change: He could ask what aspect of speech has whole-number multiples instead. The answer is the harmonics of the vocal folds, because the folds are fixed on their edges.

exam2-review-18.answer: A **spectrogram** shows many spectra lined up one after another over time. Time runs along the horizontal axis, frequency runs up the vertical axis, and darkness shows how much amplitude there is at each frequency and time. The **formants show up as dark bands**, so you can follow them rising and falling as the speaker changes sounds. For example, from /i/ to /a/ the F1 band rises and the F2 band falls.
teaching: A **spectrum shows one instant**, while a **spectrogram shows how the spectrum changes over time**.
On a spectrogram, black means high amplitude, gray means medium amplitude and white means low amplitude.
Speech is never one steady vowel, so the formants are always moving. A spectrogram makes that movement visible.
exam2-review-18.change: He could ask how a spectrum and a spectrogram differ. A spectrum shows one moment, and a spectrogram shows many moments over time. He could also ask what the dark bands are, and they are the formants.

exam2-review-19.answer: At that location the air must be **very springy and barely moving** in that mode. A constriction raises both the mass and the stiffness of the air there. The formant went up a great deal, so the added stiffness must be what counted. Stiffness only counts where the air compresses and expands, and the added mass did nothing because the air there was not moving.
teaching: A **constriction** (narrowing) of the vocal tract always raises both the mass and the stiffness of the air there. **Compressing air makes it stiffer**, and packing more air into one spot makes it heavier.

Which effect counts depends on **whether the air in that mode is moving or compressing at the constriction**. If the air is compressing there, the formant goes up. If the air is moving there, the formant goes down.
In /i/, the constriction two thirds of the way up the tract is at a moving spot for Mode 1 and a springy spot for Mode 2. So **F1 goes down and F2 goes up**.
exam2-review-19.change: He could ask about the opposite case, a constriction that lowers a formant a great deal. That means the air there is moving a lot and barely compressing, as at the lips for /u/.

exam2-review-20.answer: The network has **three hidden layers**, with three, two and four neurons. It has five layers in all, which are the input layer with two neurons, the three hidden layers and the output layer with five neurons. There are only four Linear lines, because the input layer does no calculations and so gets no line of code.
teaching: In PyTorch, each **nn.Linear** line describes one layer that does calculations. Its first number is how many values come in, and its second number is how many neurons the layer has.
The second number of the **last line** is the **output layer**. So the hidden layers are the second numbers of every line except the last.
Each layer's number of outputs must match the next layer's number of inputs, so the numbers can pass all the way through the network.
exam2-review-20.change: He could give a longer or shorter Sequential, or one with nn.Sigmoid lines in between. Sigmoid lines are not layers, so count only the Linear lines. He could also ask how many layers there are in total, and then the input layer counts too.

exam2-review-21.answer: Change the old last line from 4 in and 5 out to **4 in and 3 out**, and then add a new last line that takes **3 in and gives 5 out**. The first three lines stay the same. The new hidden layer of three neurons now sits right before the output layer, and every layer takes in exactly as many numbers as the layer before it gives out.
teaching: Adding a layer means adding one Linear line and **fixing the sizes on both sides of it**. So the line before the new layer must output three numbers, and the new line must take in three numbers.
Writing PyTorch from scratch and getting every dot and bracket right is not the skill being tested. Changing the layer sizes so they match is the skill being tested.
exam2-review-21.change: He could ask for an extra layer right after the input, or for a new layer with a different number of neurons. In every case, the numbers must match where one line meets the next.
